title: A Couple Stole Our Airplane Seats and Gloated, Then the Whole Cabin Turned on Them
excerpt: My ex-husband, Greg, had a habit of treating every detail of a trip like an impending disaster while simultaneously causing half the problems himself.
author: admin

blocks.text: My ex-husband, Greg, had a habit of treating every detail of a trip like an impending disaster while simultaneously causing half the problems himself.

We were flying from Dallas to Seattle for his sister’s fortieth birthday. We had booked our tickets three months earlier. I paid an extra fee to select row 14, seats B and C, specifically because Greg was six-foot-two with chronic lower back stiffness, and I wanted an aisle seat so I could stand up and stretch without crawling over a stranger.

We were almost the last passengers down the jet bridge because Greg had misplaced his boarding pass at the gate coffee shop. He tore through his jacket pockets, his backpack, and his wallet, muttering under his breath and blaming the gate agent for rushing him. By the time we walked back to the counter, found the paper stub sitting right next to the napkin dispenser, and got our barcodes scanned, the overhead chime had already sounded for final boarding.
I pulled my rolling bag down the narrow aisle, clutching our passes in my hand. The cabin was warm, smelled of pretzels and damp raincoats, and every overhead bin looked crammed shut.

Row 14 had three seats on the right side. Sitting right there in seats B and C was an older couple, probably in their early seventies. The man had a golf visor pulled low over his forehead, and the woman had a beige cardigan draped over her shoulders.
Between them, occupying the window seat 14A, was the woman’s oversized quilted tote bag, along with a thick winter coat spread out over the cushion.
They had taken all three seats for the two of them.
I checked our printed passes again just to be certain. “Excuse me,” I said politely, offering a gentle smile. “I think you might be in our seats. We have 14B and 14C.”
The man did not even lift his head. He just tapped his crossword puzzle with a miniature pen. “We’re comfortable here,” he said flatly.
I thought he was making a dry joke, so I let out a small, polite chuckle. “No, really. These are our assigned seats. Row 14.”

The woman turned to look at me then. Her eyes were sharp, scanning my face, my casual sweater, and Greg hovering anxiously behind me in the aisle. “There are open seats right in front of us,” she said, waving a hand toward row 13 as if shooing a fly. “Go sit there.
We’re already settled, and we have bad knees. Moving our things now is ridiculous.”
Row 13 had three seats. In 13A, next to the window, sat a very young, petite girl wearing oversized headphones, staring out at the tarmac with a notebook on her lap. Seats 13B and 13C were empty.
“Ma’am, we paid for these specific seats months ago,” Greg spoke up, his voice pitching high with irritation. “You need to move.”
“We are senior citizens,” the woman snapped, her voice carrying down the aisle. “You two are young enough to step around. Show some respect and take row 13.”
Other passengers started peeking around their headrests. A flight attendant hurried up from the front galley, squeezing past the beverage cart. Her name badge read Brenda.
“Is everything all right here, folks? We need the aisle clear so we can close the cabin door,” Brenda said, her tone strained.
“These people took our seats,” Greg said, shoving our passes forward. “We have 14B and 14C. They refuse to get up.”
Brenda looked at the older couple. “Sir, ma’am, may I see your boarding cards?”
The woman sighed with theatrical exhaustion. She dug slowly into her purse, pulled out two wrinkled stubs, and handed them over. Brenda looked at them, and I saw her mouth tighten.
“You’re assigned to row 27,” Brenda said quietly. “Those are two middle seats near the rear.”

“Well, my husband has sciatica,” the woman declared loudly, ensuring the entire middle cabin heard her. “And my hip has been acting up since security. Row 27 is right next to the lavatories, and people bump into you the entire flight. We cannot walk all the way back there. There are two empty seats right in front of this young couple. Why are you harassing two elderly people when you have open seats right here?”
Greg’s face turned mottled red. “Because in an emergency, manifests matter. If there’s an accident, our names aren’t in the right locations! That’s an FAA safety issue!”
He was technically right, but the way he yelled it made a mother across the aisle pull her toddler a little closer.

Brenda looked at Greg, then at me, then at the older couple, who had crossed their arms with stubborn defiance. The gate agent was already tapping on the airplane door from outside, signaling that they needed the departure clearance immediately.

Brenda took a steadying breath and looked at me with clear pleading in her eyes. “Sir, ma’am, if you wouldn’t mind taking row 13, I will manually update the digital manifest on my tablet right now so your names are registered to 13B and 13C. It will keep us on schedule, and you will actually have more legroom because row 13 has a slightly wider pitch.”
Greg started to argue again, his neck veins bulging, but I put a hand on his forearm. The entire plane was glaring at us, wishing we would just sit down so we wouldn’t miss our takeoff slot.
“Fine,” I told Brenda. “We’ll take row 13.”

Greg huffed, muttering furiously under his breath as he shoved our carry-on bags into the only open bin two rows ahead. We slid into 13B and 13C. The slim girl by the window barely looked up, tucking her elbows neatly to her sides and giving us plenty of space. She didn’t take up an inch of our room.
I buckled my seatbelt, trying to let the frustration drain out of my shoulders. But just as the flight attendants began their safety demonstration, the voices behind us rose.
“Told you,” the older man chuckled loudly, leaning back into his stolen seat. “All you have to do is hold your ground. People fold every single time.”

“Look at all this space, Harold,” his wife replied, not bothering to lower her voice at all. “We have the entire row to ourselves. We can stretch right out for the next four hours. Those two looked like they needed to learn some manners anyway.”

Greg gripped his armrest until his knuckles went bone white. I stared straight ahead at the plastic tray table in front of me, listening to them laugh, realizing they had deliberately stolen our row just to get a private three-seat lounge for free.
For the first forty-five minutes of the flight, the couple in row 14 made sure everyone around them knew how clever they were.

The husband, Harold, stretched his long legs straight across the empty floor space of seat 14A. His wife, whose name I learned was Evelyn, spread her knitting, a paperback thriller, and an assortment of hard candies across the unoccupied middle tray table. Whenever Brenda or the other attendant walked past, Evelyn would beam sweetly and ask for extra napkins or an extra pillow, basking in the luxury of their self-appointed first-class row.

“It’s just common sense,” Evelyn said loudly to a woman sitting across the aisle in 14D. “When you get to our age, you have to look out for yourself. Airlines pack people in like cattle nowadays. If you don’t take what’s open, nobody is going to hand it to you.”
The woman in 14D offered a tight, uncomfortable nod and quickly turned her attention back to her iPad.

Greg was simmering. Every time Harold shifted his feet or Evelyn laughed, Greg’s knee started bouncing against the carpet. “I ought to turn around and tell them exactly what kind of cheap grifters they are,” he whispered through gritted teeth.

“Greg, don’t,” I murmured. “It’s done. We’re in row 13. The girl next to us is quiet, we have plenty of room, and making a scene at thirty thousand feet is only going to get us met by airport police.”

The girl at the window, who had one ear of her headphones slipped off, glanced over at us. She gave me a sympathetic, knowing little grimace, then went back to sketching in her notebook. She really was the ideal seatmate, small and unobtrusive, which was the only silver lining keeping my blood pressure from spiking.
An hour into the flight, the captain turned off the fasten seatbelt sign, and the flight attendants began the drink service.

Brenda pushed the cart down the aisle. When she reached row 13, she stopped and gave Greg and me a warm, genuine smile. “Can I get you two something to drink? And please, take whatever snacks you’d like from the premium basket. It’s on the house, as a thank you for your patience earlier.”

Greg ordered a gin and tonic, and I asked for a sparkling water and a bag of roasted almonds. Brenda handed them over with an extra pack of shortbread cookies. She was clearly trying to make amends for having to appease the bullies behind us, and I appreciated the gesture.
Then Brenda rolled the cart back one step to row 14.
“And what can I get for you folks?” Brenda asked, her professional customer-service voice slipping back into place, cool and polite.
“We’ll take two red wines,” Evelyn declared promptly. “And two of those cheese and fruit platters from the fresh menu.”
Brenda pulled the small bottles of Merlot from the cart and placed two plastic cups on Evelyn’s tray. Then she reached into the refrigerated drawer and set down the two cheese boxes.
“That will be thirty-four dollars total,” Brenda said, holding out the handheld card reader.
Evelyn blinked at her. “Pardon me? Didn’t you just give them free drinks and premium snacks?” She pointed her finger directly between the gap of our seats, aiming at the back of Greg’s head.

“Those passengers had reserved and paid for their specific seats months in advance,” Brenda replied evenly. “They kindly relocated to resolve a boarding delay. Complimentary service is at the crew’s discretion.”
Harold scoffed, pulling a leather wallet from his jacket. “Unbelievable. Nickel-and-diming pensioners. Here, swipe the card.”
Brenda ran the transaction, handed Harold his receipt, and moved on down the aisle.

Evelyn tore open her cheese box with unnecessary force. “The nerve of that girl,” she complained to Harold. “Giving freebies to people who threw a tantrum at the gate, while we pay full fare. That’s modern customer service for you. No respect for our generation.”

She wasn’t whispering. Several passengers in rows 12 and 15 turned their heads, their expressions souring. People had been willing to overlook the seat swap during boarding because no one wanted a delay, but Evelyn’s constant self-righteous commentary was wearing everyone’s patience thin.

About thirty minutes later, Harold decided he needed to use the restroom. Because he had commandeered the middle and window sections, he had to climb over Evelyn’s knitting supplies and purse, bumping his hip against the back of Greg’s seat as he squeezed into the aisle. Greg didn’t say a word, but he gripped his magazine so hard the paper tore.
While Harold was gone, the seatbelt sign flashed back on with a double chime.
“Folks, from the flight deck,” the captain announced. “We’re anticipating some moderate chop over the Rockies. Flight attendants, please secure the cabin and take your jumpseats.”
Brenda immediately walked down the aisle, checking overhead bins and ensuring tray tables were locked. She stopped at row 14.
